name: Valdivia culture
capital: No capital (sites such as Real Alto)
summary: One of the oldest settled cultures in the Americas, on the coast of Ecuador. It made some of the earliest pottery in the Americas and small stone and clay “Venus” figurines.

location.value: The coast of the Santa Elena peninsula, Ecuador.

terrain.value: A dry coastal strip in south-west Ecuador (Santa Elena Peninsula), cut by river valleys with wetter soils.
terrain.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

climate.value: Tropical dry coast, affected by El Niño.
climate.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

resources.value: Fish and shellfish from the sea and mangroves; maize, beans, squash and cotton grown in the valleys.
resources.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

disasters.value: El Niño years brought heavy rain and floods to this normally dry coast and disturbed fishing.
disasters.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

population.value: No reliable estimate; villages such as Real Alto may have held a few hundred to over a thousand people.
population.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

urbanisation.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

disease.value: Unknown; no written records, and skeletons have not given a clear picture of disease.
disease.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

migration.value: Unknown; Valdivia grew out of earlier local peoples (the Las Vegas culture) rather than newcomers.
migration.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

economicBase.value: Fishing and early farming (maize, beans, cotton).
economicBase.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

tradeRoutes.value: Exchanged spondylus (thorny oyster) shells and other goods along the coast and inland, possibly as far as Peru.
tradeRoutes.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

wealth.value: No estimate is possible; there is little sign of large differences in wealth.
wealth.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

moneyAndTax.value: No money or taxes are known; goods were exchanged or shared.
moneyAndTax.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

inequality.value: Mostly equal farming villages; some later houses and burials suggest emerging leaders.
inequality.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

governmentType.value: Village communities, probably led by elders or kin-group leaders rather than kings.
governmentType.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

keyRulers.value: No rulers are known; there was no writing to record names.
keyRulers.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

succession.value: Unknown; leadership was probably based on kinship and age.
succession.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

institutions.value: Villages built around open ceremonial plazas, used for gatherings and rituals.
institutions.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

stability.value: Remarkably long-lasting: the same way of life continued for about 2,000 years (about 3500–1500 BCE).

eliteConflict.value: Unknown; there is no clear evidence of rival elites.
eliteConflict.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

armyAndTech.value: Unknown; there is little evidence of warfare or special weapons.
armyAndTech.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

majorWars.value: No wars are known from the archaeological record.
majorWars.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

territoryChange.value: Spread along the coast of Ecuador and into nearby valleys; no evidence of conquest.
territoryChange.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

alliancesRivals.value: Unknown; contacts with neighbours were probably through exchange rather than alliances.
alliancesRivals.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

inventions.value: Some of the earliest pottery in the Americas.
inventions.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

scienceEducation.value: No writing; knowledge of farming, fishing and pottery was passed on by example and word of mouth.
scienceEducation.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

openness.value: Unknown, though shell exchange shows contact with other regions.
openness.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

communicationTransport.value: Canoes and rafts along the Pacific coast; travel on foot to inland valleys.

religion.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

languageWriting.value: No writing; the language they spoke is unknown.
languageWriting.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

artsArchitecture.value: Small stone and clay female figurines (“Valdivia Venuses”) and some of the oldest pottery in the Americas.
artsArchitecture.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

socialStructure.value: Households grouped in oval houses around a plaza; probably organised by kinship.
socialStructure.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

sharedIdentity.value: A shared pottery and figurine style across many villages suggests a common culture.
sharedIdentity.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

dailyLife.value: Oval houses of wood and cane with thatched roofs, arranged around a central plaza; fish, shellfish, maize and beans.

neighbours.value: Followed the Las Vegas culture on the same coast; later followed by the Machalilla culture.
neighbours.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

ideasReligions.value: Unknown; figurines may have been used in fertility or healing rituals.
ideasReligions.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

colonisation.value: None; it did not settle colonies abroad.
colonisation.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

riseSignals.value: Appeared a thousand years after the Las Vegas culture.

peakPeriod.value: The 3rd millennium BCE, when villages such as Real Alto grew larger.
peakPeriod.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

declineSignals.value: Gradually changed into the Machalilla culture, rather than collapsing.
declineSignals.source: Raymond, in Silverman & Isbell (eds), Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

outcome.value: Ended about 1500 BCE; followed by the Machalilla culture.

overallCertainty.value: Low to medium. Second source: Wikidata ends it c. 1800 BCE; Wikipedia gives c. 1500 BCE.

knownFor.label: Valdivia figurines
knownFor.note: Small female figures in stone and clay.

knownFor.label: Early pottery
knownFor.note: Some of the oldest pottery in the Americas.
